title: Microeconomics Adventure 3: Market Structures
welcome_lead: Today you'll tour the four market structures from perfect competition to monopoly.
meta_desc: Economics: perfect competition, monopolistic competition, oligopoly, monopoly.
final_note: You compared four market structures by number of firms, barriers and pricing power.

concepts.def: Many firms, identical product, no power
Share of top N firms in industry

walkthroughs.body_html:
Perfect competition: many firms, homogeneous product, perfect information, free entry. Each firm a price-taker; long-run normal profit only.

Monopolistic competition: many firms, differentiated products (Chamberlin 1933). Some pricing power; long-run normal profit, but not productively or allocatively efficient.

A few large firms dominate. Decisions are interdependent — one firm's price cut triggers rivals.

Models: kinked demand (Sweezy 1939) explains sticky prices; game theory models strategic moves (HL).

Collusion (cartels, OPEC) is profitable but unstable and often illegal.

A single seller with high barriers to entry (patents, network effects, natural monopoly).

Price > MC → allocative inefficiency, deadweight loss.

Possible benefits: economies of scale, innovation funded by abnormal profit.

mcqs.q: Why do economists generally argue against protectionism?
options: Tariffs and quotas raise prices for consumers, protect inefficient industries, invite retaliation, and reduce overall welfare — even when they save specific jobs, the cost per job saved typically exceeds the wage.
Protectionism means protecting national parks from development.
Protectionism always makes a country richer by keeping money at home.
A trade deficit means a country has no factories.

mcqs.q: Is a trade deficit necessarily bad?
options: Not necessarily — it can reflect strong domestic demand, attractive investment opportunities, or borrowing to fund growth. Context matters more than the headline figure.
Protectionism means protecting national parks from development.
A trade deficit always means a country is losing wealth and failing economically.
A trade deficit means a country has no factories.

mcqs.q: What components make up aggregate demand?
options: AD = C + I + G + (X - M): consumption, investment, government spending, and net exports. A shift in any component shifts the AD curve.
Aggregate demand is just the total amount consumers want to buy.
A trade deficit means a country has no factories.
Aggregate demand is the same as GDP measured by demand.
